citations.quote: A **density operator** on $H$ is a non-negative endomorphism $\rho:H\to H$ with $\operatorname{tr}(\rho)=1$
The operator $T$ is **non-negative** when $T$ is self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]] and $$\langle Tv,v\rangle\ge 0$$ for every $v\in V$.

An **ordered tensor register** consists of a finite ordered list of
finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_0,\ldots,H_{n-1}$, each
equipped with a specified ordered orthonormal basis. Its space is
$H_0\otimes\cdots\otimes H_{n-1}$, with factors retained in the displayed
order. The product basis is ordered lexicographically by its tuple of factor
indices. The empty tensor product is $\mathbb C$ with basis $\{1\}$. A
zero-dimensional factor is allowed in this mathematical construction and makes
the tensor space zero; it is not a register under
[[def-qc-register-and-computational-basis]].

The inner product is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the
second, and on elementary tensors it is

$$\left\langle\bigotimes_{k<n}x_k,\bigotimes_{k<n}y_k\right\rangle_{\otimes}:=\prod_{k<n}\langle x_k,y_k\rangle_{{\rm root},k}.$$
A function $T:V\to W$ is **linear** when $$T(au+bv)=aT(u)+bT(v)$$ for all $a,b\in F$ and $u,v\in V$. Such a function is a **linear map**, or **linear transformation**.
The **matrix of $T$ relative to $\mathcal B$ and $\mathcal C$** is the matrix $[T]_{\mathcal B}^{\mathcal C}\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ whose $j$-th column is $[T(b_j)]_{\mathcal C}$.
there is **exactly one** $\lambda : n \to F$ with $x = \sum_{i<n}\lambda_i v_i$.
This is independent of the chosen basis: matrices of the same endomorphism in two ordered bases are similar, and similar matrices have equal trace.
For a square matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$, its **trace** is the sum of its diagonal entries, $$\operatorname{tr}(A):=\sum_{i\in n}a_{ii}.$$

If $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d$ are its eigenvalues counted with multiplicity, define its **von Neumann entropy** by $$S(\rho):=-\operatorname{tr}(\rho\ln\rho):=-\sum_{j:\lambda_j>0}\lambda_j\ln\lambda_j.$$

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be linear. The following are equivalent:

1. $T$ is non-negative.
2. $T$ is self-adjoint and every eigenvalue of $T$ is a nonnegative real number.
3. Some orthonormal basis makes the matrix of $T$ diagonal with nonnegative real diagonal entries.
4. There exists a linear map $S:V\to V$ such that $T=S^*S$.

derivations.claim: For each basis vector $f_b$, prescribe $\rho_{\rm out}f_b:=\sum_{a=1}^{d_{\rm out}}(\sum_{i=1}^{d_{\rm in}}\rho_{(i,a),(i,b)})f_a$. The product basis in [F3] supplies the matrix entries of $\rho$, and [F4]–[F6] give a unique linear extension from the prescribed images; its matrix is exactly the displayed formula.

Since $\rho$ is self-adjoint by [F1]–[F2], its matrix satisfies $\overline{\rho_{(i,b),(i,a)}}=\rho_{(i,a),(i,b)}$, so $\rho_{\rm out}$ is self-adjoint. For every $y\in H_{\rm out}$, expansion in $(f_a)$ gives $\langle\rho_{\rm out}y,y\rangle=\sum_i\langle\rho(e_i\otimes y),e_i\otimes y\rangle\ge0$ by [F2]–[F3]. Its trace is $\sum_a(\rho_{\rm out})_{aa}=\sum_{i,a}\rho_{(i,a),(i,a)}=\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ by [F1] and [F7]; hence $\rho_{\rm out}$ is a density operator by [F1].

For every endomorphism $B$ of $H_{\rm out}$, define $I_{\rm in}\otimes B$ on the product basis by $(I_{\rm in}\otimes B)(e_i\otimes f_b):=e_i\otimes Bf_b$; [F3]–[F6] give its unique linear extension. For arbitrary $x,y$, expansion in the chosen bases shows this map sends $x\otimes y$ to $x\otimes By$, so it is independent of those bases. Finite matrix multiplication gives $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{\rm out}B)=\sum_{i,a,b}\rho_{(i,a),(i,b)}B_{ba}=\operatorname{tr}(\rho(I_{\rm in}\otimes B))$. The right side is therefore basis-independent. If a second choice produced $\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}$, then $\operatorname{tr}((\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}-\rho_{\rm out})B)=0$ for all $B$; taking $B$ to be the matrix unit with sole nonzero entry in row $b$, column $a$ gives $\operatorname{tr}((\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}-\rho_{\rm out})B)=(\widetilde\rho_{\rm out}-\rho_{\rm out})_{ab}$, so every entry of the difference is zero. Thus the endomorphism is basis-independent.

By [F9], $\rho_{\rm out}$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with nonnegative real eigenvalues; [F7] and step 1.2 show their sum is $\operatorname{tr}(\rho_{\rm out})=1$, so each lies in $[0,1]$. The finite spectral sum in [F8] is therefore real, with zero eigenvalues contributing $0$ by convention. Its eigenvalue multiset is intrinsic to the endomorphism, and step 1.3 proves that endomorphism is basis-independent; multiplying by the fixed real $k_B$ preserves finiteness and basis-independence.

derivations.claim: The matrix $\rho_N=I_{2^N}/2^N$ is non-negative and has trace $2^N/2^N=1$, so it is a density operator by [F2] and [F9]. Since the input factor is one-dimensional, the defining partial trace in [F1] has one summand and gives $\rho_{{\rm out},N}=I_{2^N}/2^N$.

The spectrum of $\rho_{{\rm out},N}$ consists of $2^N$ copies of $2^{-N}$. For $N=1$, $\exp(N\log2)=2$ by [F3]; if $\exp(N\log2)=2^N$, [F6] gives $\exp((N+1)\log2)=\exp(N\log2)\exp(\log2)=2^{N+1}$. Induction yields $\exp(N\log2)=2^N$ for every $N\ge1$. By [F4], $\exp(-N\log2)=1/2^N=2^{-N}$, so [F3] and injectivity in [F7] give $\log(2^{-N})=-N\log2$.
Substitution into [F1] gives $S_{\rm out}=-k_B\,2^N2^{-N}\log(2^{-N})=k_BN\log2$. Also $\log2>0$, because [F5] gives $\exp(0)=1<2=\exp(\log2)$ and [F7] is strictly increasing.

Let $c=k_B\log2>0$. For any real $M$, [F10] makes $\mathbb R$ a complete ordered field, so [F8] applied to $M/c$ supplies a natural number $N_0\ge1$ with $N_0>M/c$. For every integer $N\ge N_0$, step 2.1 gives $S_{\rm out}=cN\ge cN_0>M$, which is exactly convergence to $+\infty$.
